# Postmortem: Alembic autogenerate skipped two tables that `create_all` had already made

**Incident:** the autogenerated migration was missing two of the eight tables
**Day:** 2 of 7 (the data layer)
**Severity:** high
**Status:** resolved

---

## Summary

The autogenerated Alembic migration was missing two tables — `state_snapshots`
and `decision_records`.

They already existed in the live database, so Alembic's diff against it saw
nothing to create. **A fresh database would have been missing them entirely.**

---

## Impact

The failure mode was silent and environment-dependent:

| Database | Result |
|---|---|
| The development database, where the tables had been created by `create_all` | Worked — the migration ran, the tables were there, nothing looked wrong |
| **A fresh database** | **Missing `state_snapshots` and `decision_records`** — the migration chain could never produce the schema the application expects |

`state_snapshots` is the append-only history, one row per sync cycle.
`decision_records` is the decision audit trail. Both are tables the application
writes to on its ordinary path.

The risk was not that the development machine would break. It was that **the
schema the code expects and the schema the migrations produce were different**,
and only one of the two was ever exercised.

---

## Timeline

The documented order of events, from [`day2.md`](../progress/day2.md).

1. Day 1 left two placeholder tables in the database, created by
   `Base.metadata.create_all` at startup.
2. Day 2 replaced them with the eight-table schema the platform actually
   needs, and made Alembic the owner of the schema.
3. The migration was generated with `alembic revision --autogenerate`.
4. Alembic's autogenerate works by **diffing the models against the database as
   it finds it**. Two of the eight tables were already there — because
   `create_all` had made them — so the diff saw nothing to create and the
   migration was generated without them.
5. The migration was applied to the live database. It succeeded. The eight
   tables were present. Every check passed.
6. The defect was found by asking the question that actually matters: **would
   this migration work against an empty schema?**
7. The Day 1 tables were dropped, the migration was regenerated against an
   empty schema, and `alembic upgrade head` was verified to produce all eight
   tables.

---

## Root cause

### Autogenerate is a diff, not a declaration

`alembic revision --autogenerate` does not read the models and write down what
they are. It reads the models, reads the **database as it currently is**, and
writes down the difference. Two tables that were already present produced no
difference and therefore no line in the migration.

The generated migration is only correct if the database it was generated
against is empty. In this project it was not — `create_all` had been run at
startup on Day 1, and again on every subsequent boot, because the service
creates any missing table at startup.

### The schema had two owners at once

| Mechanism | Role |
|---|---|
| `Base.metadata.create_all` in [`backend/app/db.py`](../../backend/app/db.py) | Creates any table that is missing, at startup |
| `alembic upgrade head` | The intended owner of the schema |

Both were running. `create_all` is the reason the live database had the tables
at all, and therefore the reason the autogenerated migration omitted them.

The container still runs `alembic upgrade head` before serving, and **the step
is allowed to fail** — the service also creates any missing table at startup,
so a migration hiccup never blocks the boot. That is a deliberate resilience
choice, and it is also what allowed the two mechanisms to coexist unnoticed.

---

## How it was detected

By **dropping the tables and regenerating against an empty schema** — the
question *"does this migration work from nothing?"* rather than *"does this
migration run?"*

The existing verification could not have found it. The migration applied
cleanly, the eight tables were present, `alembic upgrade head` reported
success, and the application ran.

---

## Resolution

| # | Fix | Where |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Dropped the Day 1 tables and regenerated the migration against an **empty** schema | `backend/migrations/versions/5f4dd7978c4f_initial_platform_schema.py` |
| 2 | Verified that all 8 tables exist after `alembic upgrade head` on a clean database | `backend/migrations/versions/` |
| 3 | Alembic reads the URL from the environment, not from `alembic.ini` — the committed file has **no `sqlalchemy.url` at all**, so no credential can leak into version control | `backend/migrations/env.py` |
| 4 | The container runs `alembic upgrade head` before serving, and the step is allowed to fail so a migration hiccup never blocks the boot | `backend/Dockerfile` |

The initial migration `5f4dd7978c4f` (created `2026-11-20 21:22:28`) creates
eight tables: `state_snapshots`, `inventory_snapshots`, `demand_observations`,
`allocations`, `domain_events`, `alerts`, `decision_records` and
`system_health`. Two later migrations extend the chain with
`demand_forecasts`, `risk_assessments`, `prediction_evaluations`
(`a96660ddb375`) and `recommendations` (`677937a6659b`).

---

## What went well

- **The fix is the correct one.** Regenerating against an empty schema produces
  a migration that is correct *by construction*, rather than one that is
  patched to include two tables someone remembered.
- **Alembic's URL comes from the environment.** The committed
  [`backend/alembic.ini`](../../backend/alembic.ini) has no `sqlalchemy.url`
  at all, so no credential can leak into version control.
- **The migration chain is linear and readable.** Three revisions, each with a
  name that says what it adds.
- **The boot path is deliberately forgiving.** A failing migration does not
  stop the service, because a migration hiccup should not take the platform
  down.

## What went badly

- **Two mechanisms owned the schema at the same time.** `create_all` and
  Alembic were both creating tables, and the interaction between them was
  invisible until the migration was generated against a dirty database.
- **The verification asked the wrong question.** "Does the migration apply?"
  was answered yes. "Does the migration produce the schema?" was not asked.
- **The environment hid the defect.** The development database was the one
  case where the bug could not appear.
- **Nothing in the application would have failed loudly.** The missing tables
  are written to on the ordinary path, so the first symptom would have been a
  failed insert in production — not a missing schema.

---

## Action items

| # | Action | Status |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Regenerate the migration against an empty schema | **Done** |
| 2 | Verify all 8 tables exist after `alembic upgrade head` | **Done** |
| 3 | Keep `alembic.ini` free of `sqlalchemy.url` so no credential is committed | **Done** |
| 4 | Let `alembic upgrade head` fail without blocking the boot | **Done** — the service also creates any missing table at startup |
| 5 | A CI job that applies the migration chain to an **empty** database and asserts the resulting table set | **Not done** — the check was performed by hand on Day 2, not automated |
| 6 | Decide whether `create_all` should stay. If it stays, the CI job in item 5 is what keeps the two owners honest; if it goes, the boot path needs a different answer | **Not done** — the two owners are still in the codebase |
| 7 | A test that asserts the migration chain and the ORM models declare the same tables | **Not done** |
